summary: An early 1969 memo on host software for the ARPANET. It discusses how links between host computers might be organised, including a special control link that hosts would use to set up and break user links and to pass status messages. It is a working proposal from the earliest days of the network, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2 is an early outline of host software for managing ARPANET links and messages. It describes a control link for host coordination, user links, checksum checking, and functions for the host monitor.

subtitle: A working outline for host links, message checks, and network monitoring.

tldr.problem: The memo outlines host software functions needed to set up and manage links between ARPANET hosts and to handle network messages.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes control, primary, and auxiliary links, message checksums, optional positive acknowledgments, monitor functions, and executive primitives.
tldr.outcome: This is a working outline; the available copy states that its first page is missing and gives no title.

sections.title: Control, Primary, and Auxiliary Links
sections.content:
The memo distinguishes three kinds of links. A control link, logical link 0, connects each pair of hosts and carries requests to establish or break user links, status interrupts, and monitor communication.

A user may have one primary link to each other host; the remote host treats it like a teletype user, including for login. User programs may also establish multiple auxiliary links to programs on a connected host. Auxiliary links can carry binary or character data and are local to the subsystem that opened them.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal sets aside a control link for host-to-host coordination. Users and programs use separate primary and auxiliary links for their work.

sections.title: Establishing a Link
sections.content:
To connect host A to host B, A chooses an unused link and sends B a link-connect message over link 0. A waits for a reply or a timeout. If B verifies the link, the monitor returns the link number to the requester and the link is established.

If both hosts independently request the same link, the host with the higher network identification number ignores the other request and waits; the other host honors the request, verifies it, and repeats its allocation process. Auxiliary links require requests from user programs on both hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: A host requests a link over the control link and waits for verification. If both hosts make the same request, their network identification numbers determine which request proceeds.

sections.title: Checking Messages and Acknowledging Them
sections.content:
The memo proposes attaching an order-dependent checksum to each message to help locate software and hardware bugs. Its suggested method adds fields and folds carry bits into the result.

It suggests a field length of 288 bits and checksum length of 8 bits to use machine word sizes efficiently. Hosts may also enter a mode that requires positive verification of every message, with verification sent over the control link.
sections.plainLanguage: A checksum can help detect message errors. The memo also proposes an optional mode in which each message needs a positive acknowledgment.

sections.title: Monitor and Executive Functions
sections.content:
The monitor's input functions receive messages from an IMP, check their checksums, optionally acknowledge receipt, and pass messages to the recipient identified by source and link. Output functions build headers, create checksums, check link status, and send messages to the IMP.

The memo also lists functions for maintaining host and link status, answering status queries, and establishing, reading, checking, and closing primary and auxiliary links. Its initial checkout plan uses one-character messages between programs on different hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: The monitor checks incoming messages and routes them to their recipients. It also manages link status and provides functions for programs to use the links.
